Chapter 6: Focusing on Collective Results
At the very top of the team dysfunction pyramid, there’s a challenge that brings everything else together—keeping everyone focused on collective results.
Think about it: all those layers we’ve talked about—trust, healthy conflict, real commitment, and holding each other accountable—they’re all there to support one big idea.
The real win is when the team achieves outcomes that benefit everyone, not just a few individuals or specific groups.
But what happens when that focus slips away? Well, people start caring more about their own recognition, or about their department looking good, or even just about hitting a short-term target.
You might see it in small ways—a sales manager who celebrates hitting their own numbers, even if the whole company falls short. Or a project lead who keeps information close to the chest just to keep an edge.
Over time, these little moments add up. They chip away at the unity and shared purpose that make high-performing teams possible.
So, how do you keep everyone moving in the same direction?
It starts by making the team’s collective results visible and meaningful.
Here are a few ways to do that:
First, define clear, measurable goals that everyone agrees on.
What does success actually look like? And how will you know when you’ve achieved it?
Next, track progress out in the open.
Make it a habit to review key metrics and milestones together, as a group.
And don’t forget to celebrate team achievements.
When the group wins, take the time to recognize it—and make sure the recognition reflects everyone’s efforts, not just a few standout individuals.
Let’s use a simple metaphor.
Imagine a rowing team. If even one person isn’t in sync, the boat slows down. But when everyone pulls together, the team glides efficiently toward the finish line.
It’s just like that with teams at work.
Focusing on collective results means putting the team’s objectives above your own.
Leaders play a big role here.
They can reinforce this mindset by linking rewards and recognition to group achievements, not just individual ones.
When someone gets distracted by their own agenda, a good leader calls it out and brings the focus back to the team.
And most importantly, leaders need to model selflessness—showing that sometimes, you’ve got to put the group’s needs ahead of your own.
There are some practical ways to make all this stick. For example, use team scoreboards—visual displays that show how you’re progressing toward shared goals.
Or set up joint problem-solving sessions, so the team tackles obstacles together instead of pointing fingers.
When everyone consistently puts collective results first, something great happens.
The team builds a culture of shared purpose and real mutual support.
Not only does this drive better outcomes, but it also makes work more meaningful and satisfying for everyone involved.
